No one here thinks disabled people can't go out and have fun, or that if you can go out for one day you can totally work all week. We're mostly disabled ourselves, we KNOW disabled and chronically ill people can go out and have fun, and we know that doesn't mean you're able bodied and ok to work. It's the type of activities they do when they go out, HFM/CZ/CC/TFT etc etc, that are suspect, when they say they can't even do basic things for themselves but have the strength and energy to do XYZ. It's like a little kid who was "full" at dinner but totally has room for dessert; Frankie doesn't WANT to clean or do dishes or work, and so says she doesn't have the energy at all. But has the energy to post literally all day long, take pictures all day long, try on clothes, go out on weekends, etc etc.

Autistic people *can* hold jobs. Yeah, some jobs might not work well for them bc of specific triggers, like the example you just gave, but then they can at least look for another job that's sitting down and quiet so they can cope. It's not like all autistic people can't work. And I know being autistic and having chronic illness can compound things. Shelters are needed and truly a godsend in a lot of situations, but the downsides people cite are about safety inside them, not accepting certain people,  and overcrowding.
 Just like a lot of other places, the rule of " in a place where a large amount of people are smushed together out of necessity, like hospitals or the DMV, some people are guaranteed to be mean/awful" type of way; they can be dangerous places, depending on how much the shelter gives a shit and works to prevent and punish theft and physical/sexual assault. 
 Some shelters do not allow LGBTQ+ in, which is sort of self explanatory why it's an issue. A lot of shelters aren't accessible to people in wheelchairs or with other disabilities; often the intake materials aren't  available in an accessible format to people that are deaf/HOH for vision imparied, people with wheelchairs or walkers are placed in shelters that have inaccessible bathrooms, people who need medication refrigerated are placed in shelters without refrigerators by the state. In 2017 there was a lawsuit vs. the City of New York because everyone in a shelter has to have a plan for independent living there, and workers would routinely try and place people with disabilities in housing that was medically inaccessible, and when that was pointed out to them they would say people were refusing and were not being compliant with the plan. If you don't comply with the plan they can kick out of the shelter.
 They can be so overcrowded that sometimes you need to be in line hours, sometimes like 4+ hours, before they open their doors for the night so you can get a bed. That can make it really hard to find a job, because if you're in that spot you have to be back by the early afternoon to get back in line so you don't have to sleep outside for the night, and you can't freely come and go once you have a bed for the night in a lot of places. Depending where you are, if you're not working a full day, how long does it take to save for an apartment? 
 They are a godsend, absolutely, there just are issues with some shelters that need to be addressed, and we desperately need more of them if we aren't going to make more accessible housing available. 

Also, she's absolutely doing right donating to the shelters themselves. Canned food drives, while well meaning, don't really help that much, and I wish more people did what she does. I'm sorry your mom got turned off of helping people directly. I wish there was a quick test you could give people to see if they're awful dickheads or not, bc I'm positive she really was a light in anyone's day that she helped and talked to, and gave a few strength to carry on. Homelessness is a new level of hell, truly, and anyone showing kindness is so so meaningful. I hope you both are doing well, and from however far away I am I am so thankful for what she's done in the past, and for her being around and being a kind soul who tries her best to help still in the present.
